title: Horizons: Initiative
tagline: A full day on the engine room, where strategic intent becomes a product (Ch 6).
format: One-day course · Day 2 of 3 · sold singly or as a 3-day bundle
audience: Business analysts, product owners and product managers who work on funded initiatives and need to turn strategic intent into a product vision, a customer-centred feature set and a roadmap that learns.
outcomes: Explain how the analyst's role changes once an initiative is funded.
Write a product vision that connects the strategic outcome to customers and capabilities.
Build an impact map from goal to actors, impacts and deliverables.
Order features by value, risk and learning, each with a hypothesis and signal.
Plan an outcome-based roadmap and the feedback loops that keep it honest.

Top five features ordered, each with a hypothesis and signal

caseStudy.title: Delivered right first time: last-mile reliability
caseStudy.summary: Southern Cross Freight is a fictional national parcel and freight carrier moving around 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% of consignments arrive within their promised delivery window, 9% fail at the first delivery attempt, and receivers and shippers chase status through the contact centre. The target outcome is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better within 12 months, with 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%. Across the three days we follow this one idea from investment decision (Strategy), through a funded initiative and product (Initiative), to a single elaborated backlog item (Delivery).
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

modules.title: Day 1 recap · horizon bridge
modules.subtitle: From 'should we?' to 'what will we change, for whom, in what order?'

participant.bigIdea: The Initiative Horizon is the engine room: strategy goes in, a product that can learn comes out.
participant.overview:
We open by recapping Day 1 — the agile mindset, the three horizons and the lean business case — and then cross the bridge. Yesterday the (illustrative) portfolio board approved Option B, phased: a delivery-management platform with a receiver-notification and real-time booking MVP first, then at-risk flagging and dynamic route optimisation. Today we turn that intent into a product.

If you did not attend Day 1, this block gives you everything you need: the horizons model, the running case and the funded outcome. Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.
objectives: Recall the three horizons and what distinguishes them.
Summarise the funded initiative and its strategic outcome.
Identify what carries over from Strategy and what is new at Initiative.

keyPoints.title: What carries over
keyPoints.body: The outcome (≥92% on-time last-mile delivery), the hypothesis, the riskiest assumptions and the stop signals.

keyPoints.title: What's new
keyPoints.body: Customers and users in detail, product boundaries, features, a roadmap and product-level metrics.

keyPoints.title: Feedback gets faster
keyPoints.body: From quarterly business results to fortnightly or monthly product signals.

sections.heading: Day 1 in five lines
sections.body:
- Agile analysis is sized to the decision in front of you.
- Three horizons: Strategy (should we?), Initiative (what will we change or build?), Delivery (what's next and is it done?).
- At Strategy we wrote a solution-free problem statement and an outcome with a baseline.
- We mapped assumptions and tested the riskiest first.
- We wrote a lean business case that names what would prove it wrong.

sections.heading: The funded initiative
sections.body:
| Item | Carried forward (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Outcome | On-time last-mile delivery 79% → ≥92% in 12 months; status calls −40% |
| Recommendation | Option B: buy delivery-management platform, integrate with shipper and subcontractor systems via middleware, phased |
| Phase 1 | Receiver delivery-window notification and real-time booking MVP |
| Phase 2 | At-risk flagging and dynamic route optimisation |
| Key insight | The failed first attempt was the default way to find out a receiver wasn't home |
| Decision point | Week 12 — % complete at booking, first-attempt failure rate |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: Crossing the bridge
sections.body:
At Initiative the analyst's questions change:

| Strategy asked | Initiative asks |
|---|---|
| Is this worth doing? | Who exactly must behave differently for the outcome to happen? |
| What options exist? | What product or change will we deliver, and what's in and out? |
| What's the value at stake? | Which features deliver the most value soonest? |
| What would prove us wrong? | What signal will each feature produce, and when? |

activities.title: Bridge check
activities.instructions: Bring the funded initiative you'll use today (or adopt the running case). Write the strategic outcome it serves and the one assumption you'd most like to test first.

participant.aiPrompt: I'm moving a funded investment from the Strategy Horizon to the Initiative Horizon. From the lean business case below, extract: (1) the strategic outcome with baseline, target and date; (2) the top three assumptions still untested; (3) the stop or pivot signals; (4) five questions I should answer at the Initiative Horizon about customers, product scope and sequencing. Lean business case:

quiz.q: Which question belongs to the Initiative Horizon?
opts: Should we invest in more reliable last-mile delivery?
Who must behave differently, and what will we build to make that happen?
What is the company's five-year network strategy?
quiz.why: Initiative turns intent into a product: actors, behaviours and deliverables.

quiz.q: What should carry forward unchanged from Strategy?
opts: The strategic outcome and stop signals
quiz.why: The outcome and exit signals anchor the initiative.

takeaways: The outcome and assumptions travel with the initiative.
Initiative questions are about people, product and order.
Feedback should now arrive in weeks, not quarters.

presenter.purpose: Re-establish shared language, bring non-Day-1 participants up to speed and set up the funded initiative.
presenter.openingLine: "Good news — the board said yes. Bad news — now we have to work out what 'yes' actually means."

beats.label: Welcome and outcomes
beats.notes: Introduce Day 2 and the three leave-with artefacts.

beats.label: Day 1 recap
beats.notes: Five lines; ask two Day 1 participants for their best 'what would prove us wrong'.

beats.label: The funded initiative
beats.notes: Walk the table; read the disclaimer.

beats.label: Bridge check activity
beats.notes: Six minutes individual; quick chat waterfall of outcomes.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Expect a mix of Day 1 returners and new participants. Pair newcomers with returners for the first breakout. Remind everyone they can use the running case all day.
presenter.whatGood: Every participant has an initiative and a measurable outcome written down.
presenter.commonFailure: Participants bringing a project with no stated outcome — the fix is to have them write a provisional outcome now and flag it as an assumption.
debrief: Whose initiative has no clear outcome yet?
What assumption are you carrying in?
presenter.answerKey: **Running case:** outcome = on-time last-mile delivery ≥92% in 12 months, status calls −40%. Riskiest carried assumption = share of failed attempts that are genuinely avoidable with receiver contact (or subcontractor adoption of a common run-data feed).

modules.title: The analyst at the Initiative Horizon
modules.subtitle: Product thinking, boundaries and the product vision

participant.bigIdea: At Initiative, the analyst helps the team agree what the product is — and, just as importantly, what it isn't.
participant.overview:
Once an initiative is funded, the analyst's work shifts from decision support to **product discovery and definition**. You help the product owner and team understand customers and users, define product boundaries, articulate a product vision, and translate strategic intent into features that can be tested.

In this block you'll learn what the role involves, how to work alongside a product owner without duplicating them, and how to write a product vision for the running case.
objectives: Describe the analyst's contribution at the Initiative Horizon.
Clarify how the analyst and product owner divide and share work.
Write a product vision using a structured template.
Define product boundaries: in, out and not yet.

keyPoints.title: Product, not project
keyPoints.body: A product persists and evolves; it is measured on outcomes, not on finishing on time.

keyPoints.title: BA + PO partnership
keyPoints.body: The PO owns value decisions; the BA brings analysis depth, models and evidence to inform them.

keyPoints.title: The product vision
keyPoints.body: A short statement of who it's for, what need it meets, what it is, and how it differs from today.

keyPoints.title: Boundaries
keyPoints.body: In / out / not yet. 'Not yet' is the most useful column — it lets you say no without saying never.

sections.heading: What the analyst does at Initiative
sections.body:
Typical contributions:

1. **Understand customers and users** — personas, journeys and jobs to be done.
2. **Define the product** — vision, boundaries, key capabilities.
3. **Connect strategy to features** — impact mapping, feature hypotheses.
4. **Shape the roadmap** — sequence by value, risk and learning.
5. **Set up product feedback** — product metrics and review cadence.
6. **Prepare for Delivery** — a backlog that is ready enough to start, but not over-specified.

sections.heading: Working with the product owner
sections.body:
| Area | Product owner | Business analyst |
|---|---|---|
| Vision | Owns and communicates | Drafts, tests with stakeholders, sharpens |
| Priorities | Decides | Provides value, risk and dependency analysis |
| Customers | Represents the customer voice | Researches, models journeys, gathers evidence |
| Backlog | Accountable for ordering | Structures, refines, makes items testable |
| Stakeholders | Primary relationships | Facilitates workshops, manages detail |

In smaller teams one person may wear both hats. The point is that both sets of work happen.

sections.heading: Writing a product vision
sections.body:
A widely used template (paraphrased): *For [target customer] who [need], the [product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [current alternative], our product [key difference].*

**Running case:**

> For receivers who need their freight to arrive when promised, and the depot planners and drivers who serve them, *Right First Time* is a delivery-management service that captures complete consignment data at booking and confirms the delivery window with the receiver before routes lock. Unlike today's knock-and-hope attempts and overnight manifests, it plans around the receiver's own answer and gets consignments delivered on the first attempt.

Test the vision: can a contact-centre officer repeat it? Does it imply the outcome? Does it exclude things?

sections.heading: Product boundaries
sections.body:
| In | Out | Not yet |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time shipper booking with address validation | Warehouse management | Shipper self-service dashboard |
| Receiver delivery-window notification and confirmation | Linehaul scheduling | Dynamic route optimisation (phase 2) |
| Live consignment tracking for receivers | Pricing and billing | Parcel-locker network |
| Run data handed to subcontractor driver apps via middleware | Replacing subcontractor systems | Multilingual voice notifications |

activities.title: Vision and boundaries
activities.instructions: Write a product vision for your initiative using the template. Then fill in an in / out / not yet table with at least three items per column.

prompts.label: Product vision
prompts.placeholder: For… who… the… is a… that… Unlike… our product…

prompts.label: One stakeholder who will push back on 'out', and what I'll say

participant.aiPrompt: Help me write a product vision for a funded initiative. Use this structure: For [target customer] who [need], the [product name] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [current alternative], our product [key difference]. Produce three alternative versions with different emphases (customer, operational, regulatory). Then propose an in / out / not yet boundary table with at least four items each, and identify which 'out' item is most likely to cause stakeholder conflict. Initiative details:

quiz.q: Who is accountable for ordering the product backlog?
quiz.why: The PO decides order; the BA provides the analysis that informs it.

quiz.q: Why is a 'not yet' column useful?
opts: It lets you defer without rejecting, keeping focus
quiz.why: Deferring explicitly keeps the product focused while respecting stakeholder needs.

quiz.q: A strong product vision should…
opts: Name the customer, need, benefit and difference from today
Be at least a page long
quiz.why: It's short, customer-centred and differentiating.

takeaways: Think product, measured on outcomes.
Partner with the PO — don't duplicate them.
A vision someone can repeat beats one that's complete.
Use 'not yet' to keep focus.

presenter.purpose: Clarify the analyst's role in product definition and produce the first leave-with artefact: a product vision.
presenter.openingLine: "If I stopped a depot planner in the yard and asked what this product is for, what would you want them to say?"

beats.label: Role at Initiative
beats.notes: Walk the six contributions; ask which they do now.

beats.label: BA–PO partnership
beats.notes: Table; discuss real tensions in their teams.

beats.label: Product vision teach and example
beats.notes: Read the running case vision; apply the three tests.

beats.label: Activity: vision and boundaries
beats.notes: Pairs or trios; one plays a stakeholder who wants everything in.

beats.label: Shares
beats.notes: Two visions read aloud; group applies the tests.

beats.label: Debrief and close
beats.notes: Discuss boundary conflicts and how to say 'not yet'.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
Visions often come out as feature lists. Ask: 'which word in this tells me who it's for?' Have them read each other's visions aloud — clunky ones become obvious.

Use the roleplay for one pair in front of the group if energy allows.

roleplay.line: "If you're not replacing our driver apps, why should subcontractors care?"
roleplay.curveball: "Our per-drop pay and KPIs come from our own scan data — your product will make our completion numbers look worse."
roleplay.move: Acknowledge the pay and KPI concern, show the 'out' column (no replacement of subcontractor systems), and offer to co-design how run data and KPIs are reported in the pilot.

presenter.whatGood: Visions under 70 words that name a customer, a need and a difference from today; boundaries with a meaningful 'not yet'.
presenter.commonFailure: 'Out' column left empty because nobody wants conflict — the fix is to require at least three items and name the stakeholder affected.
debrief: What did you put in 'not yet' that a stakeholder really wants?
Could a front-line officer repeat your vision?
Where does your BA–PO split need clarifying?
presenter.answerKey: Model vision and boundaries as in sections 3–4. Good 'not yet' items defer valuable but non-essential scope (shipper dashboard, dynamic route optimisation) behind evidence from phase 1.

modules.title: Three levels of outcome
modules.subtitle: Strategic, product and delivery outcomes — and the metrics that link them

participant.bigIdea: Product outcomes are the bridge: faster than the strategic outcome, more meaningful than feature output.
participant.overview: The Initiative Horizon pursues **product outcomes** — changes in customer and user behaviour that drive the strategic outcome. This session separates the three levels of outcome, shows how each is owned and reviewed, and links your strategic outcome to product metrics you can actually measure.
objectives: Distinguish strategic, product and delivery outcomes.
Express product outcomes as observable behaviour changes.
Define a product metric with a data source, baseline and target.

keyPoints.title: Product outcomes are behaviours
keyPoints.body: Shippers book complete data; receivers confirm before route lock; drivers get run data without rekeying.

keyPoints.title: Three owners, three rhythms
keyPoints.body: Portfolio owns the strategic outcome, the PO owns product outcomes, the team owns delivery metrics.

keyPoints.title: The behaviour test
keyPoints.body: If you can't picture someone doing something differently, it's an output, not an outcome.

sections.heading: Three levels of outcome
sections.body:
| Level | Running case example | Who reviews |
|---|---|---|
| Strategic | On-time last-mile delivery ≥92% | Portfolio board, quarterly |
| Product | % of consignments booked with complete, validated data; receivers confirming before route lock | PO and initiative steering, monthly |
| Delivery | Notification response rate; drop-off by step | Team, every iteration |

Product outcomes are the bridge: they move faster than the strategic outcome and are more meaningful than feature output.

sections.heading: Writing a product outcome
sections.body:
A usable product outcome has four parts:

1. **Actor** — who behaves differently (receiver, shipper, driver, planner).
2. **Behaviour** — what they do that they don't do today.
3. **Measure** — the metric, its definition and data source.
4. **Target and time** — baseline → target by when.

*Example:* receivers (actor) confirm a delivery window or safe drop before the 5 am route lock (behaviour), measured as % of notified receivers responding, from the notification platform (measure), from 0% to ≥70% by week 8 of the pilot (target and time).

sections.heading: Outputs in disguise
sections.body:
| Written as | Why it's an output | Rewritten as an outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Launch the receiver app | Describes our work | ≥70% of notified receivers confirm before route lock |
| Integrate with subcontractors | Describes a deliverable | Subcontract drivers start runs with complete data, no rekeying |
| Deliver booking API | Describes a feature | ≥60% of pilot consignments booked complete on day 1 |

Worked example from another industry: a hospital outpatient team's output is *'online booking live'*; the product outcome is *'patients reschedule rather than no-show'*, measured by no-show rate per clinic.

activities.title: Link outcomes to metrics
activities.instructions: For your initiative, write one strategic outcome, two product outcomes and one delivery metric for each product outcome. Then set your review rhythm.

participant.aiPrompt: Given the strategic outcome and product vision below, propose two to three product outcomes expressed as changes in customer or user behaviour (actor, behaviour, measure, baseline → target by when). Flag anything I've written that is really an output and rewrite it. For each product outcome, suggest one delivery-level metric the team could see every iteration. Inputs:

quiz.q: A fintech is building digital onboarding. Which is a product outcome?
opts: Customer acquisition cost falls 20% this year
% of new customers who complete onboarding with verified ID in one session
quiz.why: It's a behaviour change at product level that drives the strategic outcome.

quiz.q: Which of these is an output, not an outcome?
quiz.why: Integration is work we do; the outcome is the behaviour it enables.

takeaways: Product outcomes are behaviour changes that drive strategy.
Every outcome names an actor, a behaviour, a measure and a target.
Rewrite outputs until you can picture someone acting differently.

presenter.purpose: Establish product-level outcomes before techniques, so features can later be tied to signals.
presenter.openingLine: "The board will look at on-time delivery every quarter. What will *you* look at every fortnight?"

beats.label: Three levels of outcome
beats.notes: Use the table; ask for a product outcome from someone's initiative.

beats.label: Writing a product outcome
beats.notes: Build the four-part example live.

beats.label: Outputs in disguise
beats.notes: Run the table as a quick-fire: output or outcome?

beats.label: Activity: link outcomes to metrics
beats.notes: Individual; 15 minutes.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Chat waterfall of product outcomes; apply the behaviour test to three.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Participants often write outputs as product outcomes; use the 'is it a behaviour?' test relentlessly. Keep the teach brisk so the activity gets its full 15 minutes.
presenter.whatGood: Product outcomes phrased as behaviour changes with a metric and data source.
presenter.commonFailure: 'Launch the app' as a product outcome — the fix: 'who does what differently once it launches?'
debrief: What behaviour must change for your strategy to work?
Which of your outcomes failed the behaviour test first time?
presenter.answerKey: **Running case:** product outcomes — ≥60% of pilot consignments booked with a validated address and receiver contact; ≥70% of notified receivers confirm a window or safe drop before route lock; subcontractors accept ≥90% of run data without rekeying. Delivery metrics — notification response rate; booking validation pass rate; middleware handoff error rate.

modules.title: Time frame and feedback
modules.subtitle: A months-long horizon, a fortnightly-to-monthly rhythm and a mix of signals

participant.bigIdea: At Initiative, every month without a product signal is a month you're flying on the business case alone.
participant.overview: The Initiative Horizon runs over months to a year. Feedback must arrive every few weeks — through product metrics, user research and releases — or the business case goes untested until it's too late. This session sets the initiative's planning time frame, its review rhythm and the mix of feedback that keeps it honest.
objectives: Set a planning time frame: firm near term, lighter beyond.
Design a review cadence where each review ends in a decision.
Combine behavioural, attitudinal, operational and financial feedback.

keyPoints.title: Months, not years
keyPoints.body: Plan in quarters with a firm next 6–12 weeks and a lighter view beyond.

keyPoints.title: Fortnightly or monthly signals
keyPoints.body: Product analytics, usability tests and operational data — reviewed on a fixed rhythm.

keyPoints.title: Reviews end in decisions
keyPoints.body: Continue, reorder, pivot or stop — a review without a decision is a status meeting.

sections.heading: Time frame and rhythm
sections.body:
A practical cadence for the running case:

- **Fortnightly:** product metrics glance in the team review.
- **Monthly:** initiative review — product outcomes vs targets, hypotheses validated or rejected, roadmap adjusted.
- **Quarterly:** report to the portfolio on the strategic outcome and the decision point (continue / pivot / stop).

The week-12 decision point from Strategy sits inside this rhythm.

sections.heading: Kinds of feedback
sections.body:
Use a mix — no single source is enough:

- **Behavioural:** analytics, funnel completion, time-in-step.
- **Attitudinal:** usability tests, receiver interviews, driver and shipper feedback.
- **Operational:** first-attempt failure rate, depot dwell time, call volumes.
- **Commercial/financial:** cost per consignment delivered.

For receivers and drivers, include accessibility and safety signals — speed is not the only measure of a good experience.

sections.heading: Leading and lagging signals
sections.body:
The strategic outcome (on-time %) is **lagging** — it moves slowly and late. Product outcomes and delivery metrics are **leading** — they move within weeks and predict the lagging one.

| Leading (weeks) | Lagging (quarters) |
|---|---|
| Notification response rate | On-time last-mile delivery |
| Booking validation pass rate | Cost per consignment delivered |
| Rekeying errors per run | Customer complaints per 1,000 |

If the leading signals aren't moving by the decision point, the lagging one won't either — that's your early warning.

activities.title: Design the monthly initiative review
activities.instructions: In your group, design a 60-minute monthly initiative review for month 2 of the running case. List the agenda items with timings, the evidence each needs (and who brings it), and the decisions the review can make. Include at least one attitudinal source (for example receiver or driver interviews) alongside the metrics.

prompts.label: Decisions this review can make
prompts.placeholder: e.g. reorder Next column, pause a feature, escalate to portfolio

prompts.label: Who must attend — and who must not be the only voice

participant.aiPrompt: For the initiative below, recommend a fortnightly / monthly / quarterly review rhythm with the decisions taken at each. For each product outcome, identify a leading signal (moves in weeks) and the lagging measure it predicts, and propose at least one behavioural, attitudinal, operational and financial feedback source. Initiative and outcomes:

quiz.q: Typical feedback cadence at the Initiative Horizon is…
quiz.why: Initiative feedback arrives in weeks through product metrics and research.

quiz.q: Which is a leading signal for on-time last-mile delivery?
quiz.why: Response rate moves within weeks and predicts first-attempt success.

takeaways: Plan firmly for 6–12 weeks, loosely beyond.
Every review ends in a decision.
Mix behavioural, attitudinal and operational feedback.
Watch leading signals to predict the lagging outcome.

presenter.purpose: Set the initiative's time frame and feedback rhythm so the roadmap later has something to respond to.
presenter.openingLine: "If your only feedback is the quarterly board report, how many months could you build the wrong thing?"

beats.label: Time frame and rhythm
beats.notes: Show the cadence; locate the week-12 decision point.

beats.label: Kinds of feedback and leading vs lagging
beats.notes: Stress accessibility and safety signals alongside speed.

beats.label: Activity: design the monthly review
beats.notes: Breakouts of 3–4; each group drafts a 60-minute initiative review for month 2.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Compare agendas; highlight groups whose review ends in an explicit decision.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Protect the breakout time. Groups default to status-update agendas — push them to name the decisions first and work backwards to the evidence.
presenter.whatGood: A review agenda with timed items, named evidence owners and explicit decisions.
presenter.commonFailure: A review that is a status update — the fix: 'what could this meeting decide to stop?'
debrief: What will you look at every fortnight?
Which decision can your review actually make?
presenter.answerKey: **Model monthly review (60 min):** 10 min product outcomes vs targets (PO, analytics); 15 min hypotheses validated or rejected since last review (BA); 10 min receiver and driver voice — three interview clips or quotes (BA/researcher); 15 min roadmap adjustments (PO decides); 10 min risks, decision-point readiness and escalations. Decisions: reorder Next, stop or pivot a feature, request portfolio decision early.

modules.title: Principles applied at this horizon
modules.subtitle: Seeing the whole product and thinking as a customer

participant.bigIdea: At Initiative, 'think as a customer' stops being a slogan and becomes a journey you can draw.
participant.overview: This block revisits the agile BA principles through the lens of product definition. We focus on the principles that most often fail at this horizon: seeing the whole product across channels and partners, thinking as a customer with real journeys, and avoiding waste in backlog creation.
objectives: Apply each principle to product definition decisions.
Spot common Initiative-horizon anti-patterns.
Choose one principle to strengthen on your initiative.

keyPoints.title: See the whole product
keyPoints.body: Shipper, depot, subcontract driver and receiver — the product spans organisations.

keyPoints.title: Think as a customer
keyPoints.body: Design for the receiver on a night shift, on a phone, possibly not fluent in English — not for the person in the meeting room.

keyPoints.title: Avoid backlog waste
keyPoints.body: A 400-item backlog is inventory, not analysis. Detail only what's next.

sections.heading: Principles at Initiative
sections.body:
| Principle | Question at Initiative | Anti-pattern |
|---|---|---|
| See the whole | Which actors and systems does the product touch end to end? | Designing only the screens we own |
| Think as a customer | What does the journey feel like for each actor? | Personas made up in a meeting room |
| Analyse value | Which features move product outcomes most? | Ordering by stakeholder seniority |
| Get real using examples | What real consignments can we walk through the product? | Abstract capability lists |
| Understand what is doable | What do subcontractor systems and middleware allow? | Discovering integration limits in sprint 6 |
| Collaborate and improve | Who co-designs with us? | Drivers consulted after design is done |
| Avoid waste | What must be detailed now vs later? | Full backlog written upfront |

sections.heading: Thinking as a receiver
sections.body: A receiver may be working shifts, juggling a job and family, using a phone, and has probably already lost a day waiting in for a delivery that never came. Product decisions that follow from that: plain language; a specific window, not 'between 7 am and 7 pm'; one-tap confirm or safe-drop choice; a clear 'what happens next' if they're out; a phone option for those who need it. These aren't nice-to-haves — they drive first-attempt success, which drives the strategic outcome.

sections.heading: When principles pull against each other
sections.body:
| Tension | What it looks like | A way through |
|---|---|---|
| Think as a customer vs avoid waste | Research every actor before building anything | Research the riskiest actor deeply; others lightly |
| See the whole vs understand what's doable | The ideal journey needs systems we don't control | Map the whole, deliver the controllable slice first |
| Get real vs analyse value | Walking every edge case delays ordering | Walk the five most common real consignments, then order |

Worked example from retail banking: a mortgage team mapped the whole broker-to-settlement journey, but delivered only the document-upload slice first — it was the part they controlled and the biggest wait.

activities.title: Anti-pattern spotting
activities.instructions: Look at your initiative through the anti-pattern column. Which two are most present? For each, write the principle it breaks and one corrective action you can take this month.

participant.aiPrompt: Review my initiative description below against these agile BA principles: see the whole, think as a customer, analyse to determine what is valuable, get real using examples, understand what is doable, stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement, avoid waste. Identify the three anti-patterns most likely to be present, explain the evidence in my description, and suggest one corrective action for each that I could take within a month. Initiative:

quiz.q: Which is an Initiative-horizon anti-pattern for 'avoid waste'?
opts: Detailing only the next few features
Writing a full detailed backlog upfront
quiz.why: Upfront detail for later features is inventory that will likely change.

quiz.q: Why does 'think as a customer' matter for the strategic outcome here?
opts: Designing for the receiver's real context lifts confirmations before route lock, which drives first-attempt success
quiz.why: Receiver confirmation before route lock is a key driver of on-time last-mile delivery.

takeaways: The product spans actors you don't control — map them.
Customer context drives the metrics that matter.
Detail only what's next.

presenter.purpose: Make the principles concrete for product work and surface participants' real anti-patterns.
presenter.openingLine: "Picture someone who took a day of leave to wait for a delivery, then found a card in the letterbox at 4 pm. Now let's look at our product through their eyes."

beats.label: Principles table
beats.notes: Ask which anti-pattern they've seen this year.

beats.label: Thinking as a receiver
beats.notes: Walk the receiver context; link each design choice to confirmation before route lock.

beats.label: When principles conflict
beats.notes: One tension, one way through.

beats.label: Anti-pattern activity
beats.notes: Individual.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Collect the most common anti-pattern on the board.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Post-lunch slot: keep energy up with a quick poll: 'Which anti-pattern is in your project right now?'. Expect war stories — everyone has a missed-delivery anecdote; use one as a live journey example, then move on.
presenter.whatGood: Specific corrective actions with owners and timing.
presenter.commonFailure: Corrective actions like 'more engagement' — the fix: who, what session, by when?
debrief: What's the most common anti-pattern in the room?
Which corrective action will you actually do?
presenter.answerKey: Common answers: personas not based on research → run five receiver interviews; drivers consulted late → invite one subcontractor to backlog refinement; upfront backlog → archive items beyond the next quarter.

modules.title: Personas and journey mapping
modules.subtitle: Evidence-based actors and the journey where the outcome leaks

participant.bigIdea: You can't change a behaviour you haven't watched happen.
participant.overview: Before mapping features, know the people. This session builds **evidence-based personas** for the key actors and a **current-state journey map** that shows where time, effort and confidence leak — the leaks your product must fix.
objectives: Create evidence-based personas for key actors.
Map the current journey and locate the pain points that drive the outcome.

keyPoints.title: Personas from evidence
keyPoints.body: Based on data and interviews, not imagination. Include context, goals, constraints and what success looks like.

keyPoints.title: Journeys reveal leaks
keyPoints.body: Map what each actor does, thinks and feels at each step, plus elapsed time.

keyPoints.title: Actors beyond your walls
keyPoints.body: Shippers, subcontract drivers and receivers don't report to you — and they decide whether the outcome happens.

sections.heading: What a persona is for
sections.body:
A persona is a short, evidence-based portrait of one **actor** whose behaviour your initiative needs to change. It is not a marketing segment and not a wish list. Its job at the Initiative Horizon is to keep the team designing for real people — and to hand the impact map a clear 'success looks like' behaviour.

![Annotated persona card for Mia the receiver, showing seven parts: name and role, context, goals, pain points, constraints, success looks like, and an evidence strip](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/persona-anatomy.svg)

*Anatomy of a persona — seven parts, each traceable to evidence..*

sections.heading: How to build a persona
sections.body:
1. **Choose the actor** whose behaviour matters most to your product outcome (start with one; two or three is plenty for an initiative).
2. **Gather evidence first** — five to eight interviews, analytics, complaints and support logs, observation.
3. **Cluster what you found** into context, goals, pains, constraints and today's behaviours.
4. **Write 'success looks like'** as one observable behaviour — this becomes an impact on your impact map.
5. **Fill the evidence strip** and rate confidence. Any line with no evidence is an assumption to test, not a fact.

![Blank persona template with name and role, quote, six content boxes and an evidence and confidence strip](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/persona-template.svg)

*Persona template — download the printable PDF from Resources.*

sections.heading: Running case personas
sections.body:
**Mia, 34, shift-working nurse (illustrative).** Ordered a 30 kg flat-pack wardrobe online. Mostly uses her phone. Already missed one delivery while on a night shift. Wants: to know when it will arrive, or where it can be left. Constraint: can't take calls on the ward; English is her second language.

**Ravi, dispatch coordinator at a mid-sized online retailer (the shipper).** Books consignments from a spreadsheet a few times a day. Unsure of cut-offs and address rules. Wants: a clear, quick booking. Constraint: dispatch is only part of his job.

**Jess, route planner at a Southern Cross Freight depot.** Rekeys addresses that fail validation before the 5 am route lock. Wants: complete, confirmed data before planning. Constraint: subcontractor systems and per-drop KPIs.

Each persona should state the evidence it's based on (data, interviews, complaints).

sections.heading: How a journey map works
sections.body:
A journey map follows **one persona through one scenario**, stage by stage. Read across a row for the story; read down a column for everything happening at that moment. The emotion curve and the elapsed-time row usually show where the outcome leaks.

![Explainer of a journey map grid with rows for stages, does, thinks, feels, elapsed, pain and opportunity, and six build steps](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-how-it-works.svg)

*How a journey map works — the seven rows and six build steps.*

| Row | Ask | Common mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Stages | What phases would the actor name? | Using your internal process steps |
| Does | What do they physically do? | Writing what the system does |
| Thinks | What are they wondering? | Leaving it blank |
| Feels | Up or down at this moment? | Making every step neutral |
| Elapsed | How long, and how long waiting? | Ignoring waits between steps |
| Pain | What breaks? | Listing every annoyance equally |
| Opportunity | What might fix the biggest pain? | Jumping to one solution too early |

sections.heading: Running case journey
sections.body:
![Mia's current delivery journey across five stages: order, dispatch, wait, attempt, recover, with the emotion curve dipping lowest at the failed attempt](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-worked-example.svg)

*Worked example — Mia's journey. The deepest dip is the failed first attempt.*

| Step | Receiver does | Feels | Elapsed (illus.) | Pain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Order | Buys online, gets 'ships in 1–2 days' | Hopeful | Day 0 | No delivery day given |
| Dispatch | Gets generic dispatch email | Uncertain | Day 1 | Tracking says 'in transit' only |
| Waits | Nothing visible | Frustrated | Day 1–3 | Can't plan around shifts |
| Attempt | Not home; card left | Annoyed | Day 3 | Nobody asked beforehand |
| Re-delivery or collection | Drives to depot | Resigned | Day 5–6 | Too heavy for her car |

The 'attempt' row is the default-discovery insight, now felt from the receiver's side.

Your turn: use the blank template below for the persona you chose.

![Blank journey map template with six stages and seven rows](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-template.svg)

*Journey map template — download the printable PDF from Resources.*

activities.title: Persona and pain point
activities.instructions: Pick the actor whose behaviour matters most to your outcome. Using the persona template, write a short persona (context, goal, constraint, evidence). Then sketch the current journey on the journey map template and name the single biggest pain point.

prompts.label: Biggest pain point in the current journey

participant.aiPrompt: From the research notes below, draft evidence-based personas for the key actors (context, goals, constraints, what success looks like, and the evidence each claim rests on — flag claims with no evidence). Then draft a current-state journey map with steps, what the actor does, feels, elapsed time and pain. Notes:

quiz.q: What's the best evidence base for personas?
quiz.why: Evidence-based personas stop the team designing for itself.

quiz.q: The most useful column on a journey map for outcome work is usually…
quiz.why: Waits and pain show where the outcome leaks.

takeaways: Base personas on evidence.
Include actors outside your organisation.
Journeys reveal the waits that drive the outcome.

presenter.purpose: Ground the afternoon's techniques in real actors and a real journey.
presenter.openingLine: "Who in this story has the worst day — and have any of us actually spoken to them?"

beats.label: Personas: anatomy and how to build
beats.notes: Show the anatomy visual; walk the seven parts and the evidence strip. Introduce Mia, Ravi and Jess.

beats.label: Journey mapping: how it works + Mia's journey
beats.notes: Show the how-it-works grid, then the worked example; land on the 'attempt' dip.

beats.label: Activity: persona and pain point
beats.notes: Individual, using the two templates.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Two people read their pain point; check it's evidence-based.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Keep it tight — this sets up the impact map. Challenge any persona attribute that has no evidence behind it.
presenter.whatGood: Personas that cite evidence and a pain point tied to the outcome.
presenter.commonFailure: Personas built on demographics and stock photos — the fix: what does this person do, and how do we know?
debrief: Which actor do you know least about?
Where does your journey leak most time?
presenter.answerKey: Running case: Mia (receiver) — biggest pain: nobody asks before the attempt; Ravi (shipper) — unsure of address rules at booking; Jess (planner) — rekeying failed addresses before the 5 am route lock.

participant.bigIdea: An impact map turns 'we're building a front door' into 'here's whose behaviour we're changing and why'.
participant.overview: The **impact map** is this day's central artefact. It connects the goal (why) to the actors (who), the behaviour changes we need (how) and the deliverables that might cause them (what). Anything that can't trace to an impact becomes 'not yet'.
objectives: Build an impact map: goal → actors → impacts → deliverables.
Express impacts as measurable behaviour changes.
Move deliverables that can't justify an impact to 'not yet'.

keyPoints.title: Impact maps connect why to what
keyPoints.body: Goal (why) → actors (who) → impacts (how behaviour changes) → deliverables (what).

keyPoints.title: Read it right to left
keyPoints.body: Every deliverable must justify itself through an impact on an actor that moves the goal.

keyPoints.title: 'Not yet' is a decision
keyPoints.body: Deliverables without a clear impact wait for evidence — they aren't deleted, they're deferred.

sections.heading: Impact mapping
sections.body:
```
GOAL: On-time last-mile delivery ≥92%
├── Receiver (Mia)
│   ├── Impact: confirms availability or a safe drop before route lock
│   │   ├── Deliverable: SMS/email notice with one-click confirm or safe drop
│   │   └── Deliverable: plain-language delivery window
│   └── Impact: stops calling to check status
│       └── Deliverable: live tracking with SMS updates
├── Shipper (Ravi)
│   └── Impact: books with validated address and receiver contact on day 1
│       └── Deliverable: real-time booking API with address validation
└── Depot planner and driver (Jess)
    └── Impact: plans and delivers runs without rekeying or futile attempts
        ├── Deliverable: complete run data via middleware to driver apps
        └── Deliverable: at-risk flag at sort
```

Read it right to left: every deliverable must justify itself by an impact on an actor that moves the goal. Deliverables that can't do that are candidates for 'not yet'.

sections.heading: Checking the map
sections.body:
Run four checks before you call it done:

1. **External actors** — at least one actor outside your organisation.
2. **Measurable impacts** — each impact could be counted.
3. **More than one deliverable option** per impact — otherwise you've reverse-engineered a solution.
4. **A 'not yet' margin** — at least one deliverable lost its place.

Worked example from higher education: a university's goal was first-year retention. The impact 'students book an adviser in week 3' had three options — SMS nudge, timetable slot, peer mentor. The planned app was moved to 'not yet'.

activities.title: Impact map
activities.instructions: Build an impact map for your initiative (or the running case). At least three actors, one or two impacts each, and deliverables under each impact. Circle deliverables that cannot justify an impact.

prompts.label: Deliverables that couldn't justify an impact (→ not yet)

participant.aiPrompt: Help me build an impact map. Goal: [strategic or product outcome]. For the context below, propose at least three actors (including ones outside our organisation), one or two measurable behaviour-change impacts per actor, and two candidate deliverables per impact. Flag any deliverable that doesn't clearly cause an impact. Context:

quiz.q: In an impact map, 'impacts' describe…
opts: Changes in actors' behaviour that move the goal
quiz.why: Impacts are behaviour changes; deliverables are what we build to cause them.

quiz.q: An impact with only one deliverable option often signals…
opts: A solution reverse-engineered into the map
quiz.why: Real impacts usually have several ways to cause them.

takeaways: Actors and impacts before deliverables.
Every deliverable must earn its place.
'Not yet' is a decision, not a deletion.

presenter.purpose: Produce the impact map leave-with artefact.
presenter.openingLine: "We're going to build a map where every feature has to answer one question: whose behaviour does this change?"

beats.label: Impact mapping teach
beats.notes: Build the running case map live; read it right to left.

beats.label: Checking the map
beats.notes: Four checks; university example.

beats.label: Activity: impact map
beats.notes: Breakouts; visit at 10 and 20 minutes.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Collect 'not yet' deliverables; discuss surprises.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Groups often jump straight to deliverables. Insist on actors and impacts first. If a group has only internal actors, ask: 'who outside the building has to do something differently?'
presenter.whatGood: Impact maps with external actors, measurable impacts and at least one deliverable moved to 'not yet'.
presenter.commonFailure: Impacts written as features ('receiver uses the app') — the fix: what does the receiver do differently that matters to the goal?
debrief: Which actor was hardest to define impacts for?
Which deliverable lost its place?
presenter.answerKey: Model impact map as in the section. Typical 'not yet' items: shipper dashboard, chatbot, parcel-locker network — none clearly moves the goal in phase 1 without evidence.

modules.title: Story mapping and the first release
modules.subtitle: A backbone of activities, sliced into a thin first release

participant.bigIdea: The first release should cross the whole journey thinly, not one step of it thickly.
participant.overview: A **story map** lays the actor's activities out as a backbone and slices releases horizontally across it. It turns the impact map's deliverables into a first release that can produce a signal.
objectives: Lay out a story map backbone of 4–6 activities.
Slice a first release that tests the riskiest impact.

keyPoints.title: Story maps slice releases
keyPoints.body: A backbone of activities, with stories beneath, sliced horizontally into releases.

keyPoints.title: Thin and whole
keyPoints.body: A walking skeleton across every step beats a polished single step.

sections.heading: Story mapping
sections.body:
Arrange the receiver's activities as a **backbone** (Order → Get delivery window → Track consignment → Receive delivery), place user stories underneath each activity, then draw horizontal lines to slice releases.

**Release 1 (MVP) for the running case:** receiver delivery-window notification with one-click confirm or safe drop; real-time booking with address validation for pilot shippers; run data to one subcontractor via middleware; basic tracking by SMS. Everything else waits for evidence from Release 1.

activities.title: Story map backbone and first slice
activities.instructions: Write the backbone (4–6 activities) and draw your first release slice.

participant.aiPrompt: From the impact map below, suggest a story map backbone of 4–6 user activities with candidate stories under each, and a minimal first release slice that tests the riskiest impact. Explain what the slice leaves out and why. Impact map:

quiz.q: A story map's horizontal slices represent…
quiz.why: Each slice is a releasable increment across the backbone.

takeaways: Backbone first, stories second.
Slice a thin first release across the whole journey.

presenter.purpose: Turn the impact map into a releasable first slice.
presenter.openingLine: "If you could only ship one thin line across this journey, where would you draw it?"

beats.label: Story mapping teach
beats.notes: Show backbone and Release 1 slice.

beats.label: Activity: story map
beats.notes: Same breakout groups.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: How thin is your first slice?

presenter.facilitationNotes: Short block after the break — get straight into it. Push back on first slices that only cover one activity.
presenter.whatGood: A first slice touching every backbone activity.
presenter.commonFailure: Release 1 is one activity done fully — the fix: what's the thinnest version of every step?
debrief: How thin is your first slice?
presenter.answerKey: Running case Release 1 as in the section.

modules.title: Feature hypotheses and ordering
modules.subtitle: Make each feature an experiment, then order by value, cost of delay and learning

participant.bigIdea: A feature without a hypothesis is a guess; a feature with one is an experiment.
participant.overview: With deliverables mapped, every feature gets a **hypothesis** — what it should cause and how we'll know — and then a strict **order** by value, cost of delay, risk reduction and effort.
objectives: Write feature hypotheses with a measurable signal.
Order features using value, cost of delay, risk and learning.

keyPoints.title: Feature hypothesis
keyPoints.body: We believe [feature] will result in [impact] for [actor]. We'll know when [signal] reaches [threshold] by [time].

keyPoints.title: Order, don't prioritise
keyPoints.body: Priorities collapse into 'all high'. A strict order forces trade-offs.

keyPoints.title: Learning is value
keyPoints.body: Early features that test the riskiest assumption can be worth more than larger features.

sections.heading: Feature hypotheses
sections.body:
| Feature | Hypothesis | Signal and threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Receiver delivery-window confirmation | Receivers confirm availability or a safe drop when asked directly | ≥70% respond before route lock |
| Real-time booking with address validation | Shippers book complete consignments on day 1 | ≥60% of pilot consignments complete at booking by week 8 |
| Run data via middleware to subcontractors | Drivers deliver without rekeying or futile attempts | First-attempt failure rate ≤5% |
| At-risk flag at sort | At-risk consignments can be re-planned before dispatch | ≥80% of late consignments flagged; <5% false alarms |
| SMS live tracking | Receivers stop calling for status | Status calls from pilot cohort −40% |

sections.heading: Ordering features
sections.body:
Use a simple scoring discussion, not a spreadsheet war:

- **Value** — how much does it move the product outcome?
- **Cost of delay** — what do we lose per week it's not live?
- **Risk reduction / learning** — does it test a risky assumption?
- **Effort** — rough relative size.

Weighted shortest job first (cost of delay ÷ size) is a helpful lens. In the running case, receiver delivery-window confirmation ranks first: high value, high cost of delay, tests the privacy and response assumptions, modest size.

activities.title: Top five ordered features
activities.instructions: From your impact map, choose five features. Write a hypothesis and signal for each, then put them in strict order with one line of reasoning per position.

participant.aiPrompt: Act as a product analyst. For each feature below, write a hypothesis in the form 'We believe [feature] will result in [impact] for [actor]; we'll know when [signal] reaches [threshold] by [time]'. Then propose a strict order using value, cost of delay, risk reduction and relative effort, explaining each position in one line and noting which assumption each feature tests. Finally lay out a Now / Next / Later roadmap with an outcome per column. Features and context:

quiz.q: Why order features strictly rather than tagging priority High/Medium/Low?
quiz.why: Strict order prevents everything being 'High'.

quiz.q: Weighted shortest job first divides…
opts: Cost of delay by job size
quiz.why: WSJF = cost of delay ÷ size, favouring high-value small items.

takeaways: Every feature gets a hypothesis and a signal.
Order strictly; reason out loud.
Value learning — test risky assumptions early.

presenter.purpose: Turn the impact map into an ordered, testable feature set and roadmap.
presenter.openingLine: "Five features. One order. No ties. Let's find out what you really believe."

beats.label: Feature hypotheses
beats.notes: Walk the table; highlight thresholds.

beats.label: Ordering techniques
beats.notes: Four lenses and WSJF; reveal why confirmation ranks first.

beats.label: Activity: top five
beats.notes: Pairs; one challenges the order.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: One pair shares their #1 and why.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Expect resistance to strict ordering. Allow ties for 30 seconds, then insist. Watch for features with no signal.
presenter.whatGood: Five features with measurable signals; an order defended by value and learning.
presenter.commonFailure: Signals that are outputs ('feature released') — the fix: what behaviour will we see?
debrief: What's your #1 and what does it test?
Which feature was hardest to write a signal for?
presenter.answerKey: Model order: 1 receiver delivery-window confirmation; 2 real-time booking with address validation; 3 middleware run data to one subcontractor; 4 at-risk flag; 5 SMS live tracking. Rationale: 1 tests the privacy and response assumptions and attacks the biggest leak; 2 drives completeness; 3–4 depend on 1–2 data; 5 is valuable but lower cost of delay.

modules.title: The Now / Next / Later roadmap
modules.subtitle: An outcome roadmap that changes as signals arrive

participant.bigIdea: A roadmap is a statement of intent and learning, not a delivery contract.
participant.overview: The **outcome roadmap** communicates what we're trying to change Now, Next and Later — with the hypotheses and signals that will move items between columns.
objectives: Build a Now / Next / Later outcome roadmap.
Explain how signals move items between columns.

keyPoints.title: Roadmap by outcome
keyPoints.body: Now / Next / Later columns hold outcomes and hypotheses, not dates and feature lists.

keyPoints.title: Columns move on evidence
keyPoints.body: An item moves from Next to Now when the signal it depends on arrives — not when a date passes.

sections.heading: The Now / Next / Later roadmap
sections.body:
| Now (next ~6 weeks) | Next (~6–12 weeks) | Later |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome: receivers confirm before route lock | Outcome: runs delivered without futile attempts | Outcome: dynamic re-planning on the day |
| Receiver confirmation; real-time booking | Middleware run data; at-risk flag | Route optimisation, shipper dashboard |
| Signal: response rate, completeness | Signal: first-attempt failure rate | Signal: on-time %, re-plan rate |

The roadmap is a communication tool; it changes as signals arrive.

activities.title: Place your five on the roadmap
activities.instructions: Place your ordered features on Now / Next / Later with one outcome per column and the signal that would move each Next item into Now.

prompts.label: Signal that moves a Next item into Now

participant.aiPrompt: Lay out a Now / Next / Later outcome roadmap for the ordered features below, with one outcome and signal per column, and state what evidence would move each Next item into Now or push it to Later. Features:

quiz.q: Columns on an outcome roadmap usually hold…
quiz.why: Outcome roadmaps communicate intent and learning, not delivery dates.

takeaways: Roadmap by outcome, and change it as signals arrive.

presenter.purpose: Turn the ordered features into an outcome roadmap.
presenter.openingLine: "No dates on this board — just outcomes and the evidence that moves them."

beats.label: Now / Next / Later
beats.notes: Show the roadmap; point at the signals row.

beats.label: Activity: roadmap
beats.notes: Same pairs.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: What moved from Now to Later?

presenter.facilitationNotes: Expect requests for dates. Acknowledge them, then show where dates live (the Delivery Horizon), not here.
presenter.whatGood: One outcome per column, with signals that move items.
presenter.commonFailure: Columns that are just quarters with features — the fix: what outcome is each column for?
debrief: What moved from Now to Later?
presenter.answerKey: Running case roadmap as in the section.

modules.title: Exercise: apply to a funded initiative · close
modules.subtitle: Vision, impact map and five ordered features — then the bridge to Delivery

participant.bigIdea: Leave with a product the team can start building on Monday — and a way to know if it's working.
participant.overview: Consolidate the day's three artefacts for your own funded initiative: the product vision, the impact map and the top five features ordered with hypotheses and signals. Then we close and bridge to Day 3, where one of those features becomes a fully elaborated backlog item.
objectives: Finalise a product vision, impact map and ordered top five.
Check traceability from strategic outcome to feature signal.
Choose the feature you'll elaborate on Day 3.

keyPoints.title: Traceability
keyPoints.body: Outcome → actor → impact → feature → signal. Every link should be explicit.

keyPoints.title: Direct the agent
keyPoints.body: Use AI to tidy and cross-check; you own the order.

keyPoints.title: Bring one feature
keyPoints.body: Tomorrow you'll elaborate one backlog item end to end.

sections.heading: Exercise brief
sections.body:
1. Finalise your product vision (≤70 words).
2. Clean up your impact map; mark 'not yet' deliverables.
3. Confirm your top five order with hypotheses and signals.
4. Run a traceability check: can each feature be traced to an impact, an actor and the outcome?
5. Choose the feature you'll take into Day 3.

sections.heading: Bridge to Day 3
sections.body: At the Delivery Horizon the question becomes *what's the next most valuable slice, and is it done?* We'll take one feature — for the running case, receiver delivery-window confirmation — split it into stories, elaborate one with examples, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements and a value metric, and plan the week around it.

activities.title: Consolidate the three artefacts
activities.instructions: Complete each box for your initiative.

prompts.label: Top five features ordered, with hypothesis and signal

participant.aiPrompt: Check the traceability of my initiative artefacts below. For each of my top five features, confirm it links to a deliverable on the impact map, an actor impact and the strategic outcome; flag any broken links. Check each hypothesis has a measurable signal, threshold and time. Then recommend which feature is the best candidate to elaborate into a first backlog item, and why. Artefacts:

quiz.q: A traceability check at Initiative confirms that…
opts: Every feature has a test case
Each feature links to an impact, an actor and the outcome
quiz.why: Traceability from outcome to feature keeps the product aligned.

quiz.q: What's the focus of the Delivery Horizon?
opts: The next valuable slice, and whether it's done
quiz.why: Delivery is about small, finished, valuable increments.

takeaways: Three artefacts: vision, impact map, ordered top five.
Trace every feature back to the outcome.
Tomorrow: one item, fully elaborated.

presenter.purpose: Consolidate artefacts and set up Day 3.
presenter.openingLine: "Let's make sure that if someone asks 'why are we building this?', every feature can answer for itself."

beats.label: Brief
beats.notes: Explain steps.

beats.label: Individual consolidation
beats.notes: Circulate; prompt traceability.

beats.label: Shares and close
beats.notes: Two participants share their #1 feature and signal.

beats.label: Bridge to Day 3
beats.notes: Ask them to bring their chosen feature.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Keep it calm and focused. If someone's artefacts are thin, prioritise the ordered top five — it feeds Day 3 directly.
presenter.whatGood: All three artefacts present, with a chosen Day 3 feature.
presenter.commonFailure: Features that trace to no actor — the fix: drop them to 'not yet'.
debrief: Which link in your traceability chain is weakest?
Which feature will you bring tomorrow?
presenter.answerKey: Running case Day 3 feature: receiver delivery-window confirmation — highest order, tests the privacy and response assumptions, small enough to elaborate in a day.
